title: I am the bread of life (John 6:35)
hook: the first great I am: whoever comes to me shall not hunger

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pool with five porches, and a question: wilt thou be made whole? What was your honest answer? Day five hundred three.

The day before, on a hillside by the Sea of Galilee, five thousand men sat down on the grass and ate from five barley loaves and two fish, with twelve baskets left over. Then the crowd wanted to take him by force and make him king. He slipped away. Now, the next morning, they've crossed the lake in boats to find him again. And he tells them, plainly: you're looking for me not because you saw signs, but because you ate the bread and were filled. They want more breakfast. He's about to offer them something else.
screen: `FIVE THOUSAND FED ON A HILLSIDE.` → `THEY WANT TO MAKE HIM KING.` → `THEY COME BACK FOR MORE BREAD.`

segments.voice: The crowd pushes back. What sign will you give us? Our fathers ate manna in the desert; Moses gave them bread from heaven. It's a fair challenge. Yesterday's loaves were impressive, but manna fed a whole people for forty years. Jesus corrects them: it wasn't Moses who gave the bread, it's my Father who gives the true bread from heaven. And they say, almost like the woman at the well: Lord, give us always this bread. Then the line, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall not hunger: and he that believeth in me shall never thirst." John's Gospel will come back to this shape again and again: I am, and then a picture. I am the bread of life. The light of the world. The door. The good shepherd. The resurrection and the life. The way, the truth and the life. The true vine. We'll meet most of them in the weeks ahead. Each takes something ordinary and says: this is what I am to you. Bread is about as ordinary as it gets. Not a feast. Not a delicacy. The thing on the table, the thing people need day after day. Not hunger, not thirst: he's not promising they'll never miss a meal. He's speaking of a deeper hunger, the one that comes back no matter how much we eat. Catholics hear this whole chapter as pointing toward the Eucharist, and we'll go further into that tomorrow. Today, stay with the plain image. Bread is daily. The promise is daily too.
screen: `OUR FATHERS ATE MANNA.` · `LORD, GIVE US ALWAYS THIS BREAD.` · `I AM, AND THEN A PICTURE.` · `BREAD: ORDINARY AND DAILY.` · then, large: `I AM THE BREAD OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray before eating. Think of your next meal, or if food is nearby, set it in front of you. Settle, and breathe. Before the first bite, stop. Look at it. Think of the hands that grew it, carried it, cooked it. Some Catholic families say a short grace before meals, such as the old one that begins bless us, O Lord. If you pray, you can say it, or simply give thanks in your own words. If you don't, just pause and let the food be noticed before it's eaten. The bell holds the time.
Manna. What the crowd asked for, remembering the desert, before Jesus answered: I am the bread of life, and whoever comes to me shall not hunger. Today's word.
Your line: bread of life. Today, don't eat your first bite of any meal without a pause. Day five hundred three.

screen: `DAY 503 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: MY FLESH IS MEAT INDEED.`

howItsDone: Some Catholic families say a short grace before meals, and the Church reads John 6, the Bread of Life discourse, over several Sundays in late summer of Year B.

original.script: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος τῆς ζωῆς
original.say: eh-GOH ay-MEE ho AR-tos tays zoh-AYS
original.note: Greek: I am the bread of life (John 6:35).

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice metaphor about spiritual nourishment.
what it means: Jesus offers himself as the daily bread that answers the deepest hunger, and the chapter goes on toward the Eucharist.
what a scholar hears: the same Greek, egō eimi, as 'it is I' on the water in 6:20, now with a picture attached, and set against the manna of Exodus 16.

sources.quoted: I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall not hunger: and he that believeth in me shall never thirst.

notes: Seven 'I am' sayings with predicates (6:35; 8:12; 10:7/9; 10:11; 11:25; 14:6; 15:1): the standard count. Confirm.
The grace 'Bless us, O Lord' is named by its opening words only, not quoted as a source. Confirm acceptable.
Lectionary: John 6 read on the 17th–21st Sundays in Ordinary Time, Year B. Confirm.
'Not hunger' read as a deeper hunger: confirm the phrasing doesn't preempt the Eucharistic reading taught tomorrow.
Confirm exact Douay wording of John 6:35.
